actions.body:
In this analysis, we examine the relationship between computational boundaries and sequential decision models in artificial systems. By reviewing available literature, we find that structural explanations for decision paths help clarify how systems maintain continuity. 

Summary
We look at how computational systems process memory and decision-making to better understand synthetic identity.

Generative video models are evolving from tools for short-form visual synthesis into intelligent creative systems capable of shot organization, scene preservation, and preliminary narrative generation. The emergence of Seedance 2.0 exemplifies this transition. In contrast to earlier models prioritizing local visual realism, Seedance 2.0 emphasizes spatial consistency, camera motion understanding, audiovisual synchronization, and accessible production workflows. This development signifies a broader shift in generative video technology from basic image generation toward integrated audiovisual expression (
Figure 1
A).
1
Figure 1.
Open in a new tab
Evolutionary roadmap of generative video AI: From “tool” to “creator”
(A) Timeline: Evolutionary roadmap of generative video AI. (B) Capability Leap: From basic synthesis to intelligent audiovisual creation. (C) Key Challenges: Core problems driving the field forward.
However, generative video models have not yet attained the status of “intelligent directors.”
2
Although the newly released Seedance 2.5 already supports up to 30 s of multi-round rewriting and supports up to 50 channels of image, audio, and video materials, they face critical challenges in long-horizon narrative planning, character identity preservation, physi

ectively counter these capabilities, highly generalizable AI detection engines must be capable of identifying AI-generated, deeply synthesized, manipulated, or voice-altered content. For high-risk scenarios, deployment-level multimodal detection and defense must be prioritized as a key engineering objective for generative video systems rather than regarded as a resolved technical challenge.
Artistic evolution: Acceleration of the “digital renaissance”
Seedance 2.0 liberates video creators from traditional collaborative constraints and high capital requirements. AI-augmented creation enables individuals to oversee the entire production life cycle, from content generation to commercial monetization, thereby positioning the individual as a pivotal agent of innovation and advancing the democratization of creative expression. Historically, technological shifts have catalyzed, rather than diminished, artistic evolution.
We now stand at the threshold of a digital renaissance. Just as the development of linear perspective did not terminate painting but rather facilitated the emergence of Baroque and Impressionist art and as the printing press accelerated the Enlightenment and modern science, generative video AI does not supplant human creativity. Instead, it relieves creators of repetitive, foundational technical tasks. Ultimately, the future will continue to be shaped by human subjective consciousness and creative direction of algorithmic parameters.

{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=computational+boundaries+persistent+identity+memory+continuity+philosophy&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Seedance 2.0: Prospects and reflections on the evolution from “tool” to “creator”\", \"abstract\": null, \"doi\": null, \"pmid\": \"PMC13673547\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13673547\", \"source\": \"PMC\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"PubMedCentral\", \"url\": \"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13673547/?tool=EBI\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"PubMedCentral\", \"url\": \"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13673547/pdf/?tool=EBI\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13673547\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13673547?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Digital pharmaka and the crisis of subjectivation: a longitudinal phenomenological study on the educational use of technology in higher education through the philosophy of Bernard Stiegler.\", \"abstract\": \"This study investigates the ambivalent effects of digital technologies on the subjectivation processes of university students, drawing on Bernard Stiegler's philosophy of technics and the concept of the pharmakon, technology as both remedy and poison. Using a longitudinal qualitative design grounded in interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA), the research examines how digital technologies - including smartphones, social media, and AI tools - affect students' attention, memory, desires, and sense of self over an academic semester. Data from three waves of in-depth interviews and reflective journals with twelve undergraduates reveal six interrelated themes: (1) from habitual engagement to cognitive embodiment: the internalization of digital technology; (2) the fragmentation of cognitive focus: the collapse of attention regimes; (3) loss of control and addiction-like engagement: perceived dependence on digital tools; (4) disconnection from meaning: digital acceleration and its impact on memory and meaning-making; (5) Erosion of subjective integrity: identity alienation in digital learning; and (6) reclaiming the Pharmakon: moments of remedial engagement. These findings demonstrate that digital technologies not only influence learning behaviors but also restructure the symbolic, affective, and libidinal foundations of student subjectivity, while also revealing fragile but meaningful counter-tendencies through which students reclaim symbolic production and collective desire. The study extends existing empirical research by integrating lived experience with Stiegler's pharmacological lens, offering critical insights into the psychosocial and existential costs of algorithmic learning environments. It concludes by outlining implications for rethinking educational policy and pedagogy to restore attention, care, and symbolic richness in digitally mediated higher education.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1989076\", \"pmid\": \"42923245\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13687051\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1989076\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13687051\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13687051?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"The theory of psychic quanta: a quantum model for the unity of individual consciousness.\", \"abstract\": \"The Theory of Psychic Quanta (TPQ) postulates the existence of a universal non-local psychic field whose quantized excitations-termed informational quanta (analogous to qubits)-anchor to coherent brain systems to generate individual consciousness as a phenomenological unit. According to this model, the brain does not produce consciousness in an emergentist sense; rather, it acts as a bidirectional biophysical interface that stabilizes the informational quantum without generating it. This reciprocal interaction maintains experiential coherence from biological birth until the cessation of brain activity, at which point the quantum disanchors and reintegrates into the diffuse psychic field. TPQ incorporates temporal dynamics where subjective time emerges from quanta superposition collapse, unifying linear neural processing with atemporal field states. This model integrates recent updates to contemporary informational panpsychism, the Orchestrated Objective Reduction (Orch-OR) theory and Integrated Information Theory (IIT), predicting specific neurophilosophical correlates such as gamma synchronization (40-100 Hz) and inter-individual affective resonance. Predictions include EEG protocols for NDE gamma surges and past-life memory imprints in children. The theoretical implications include reinterpretation of psychological wellbeing as maximum phase coherence between the individual quantum and the universal field, explanation of non-local emotional communication between minds, and empirically verifiable predictions regarding neural patterns during empathic interactions, NDEs, telepathic intuition, and post-mortem awareness. Finally, TPQ proposes a resolution to Chalmers' \\\"hard problem\\\" of consciousness (1995) through dual ontology integrating physical-material and psychic-informational domains.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1792921\", \"pmid\": \"42253571\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13235342\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1792921\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13235342\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13235342?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"The Embodied Hijack: when Pleistocene minds meet disembodied artificial intelligence.\", \"abstract\": \"The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into everyday life has intensified a long-standing feature of human cognition: the attribution of agency, intention, and understanding to nonhuman systems. People describe language models, virtual assistants, and autonomous technologies as if these systems know, decide, want, or understand, and they continue to do so even when they know the systems have no inner life. The standard account dismisses this as naïve anthropomorphism, the misfiring of evolved agency-detection systems calibrated in the Environment of Evolutionary Adaptedness. We argue that the standard account is incomplete. It explains the immediacy of anthropomorphic response but not its persistence even when users know the system has no mind. Drawing on evolutionary psychology, philosophy of agency, and the active inference framework, we advance the Embodied Hijack hypothesis. Across evolutionary time, fluent communication and contingent responsiveness were produced only by embodied, self-maintaining agents with vulnerability and temporal continuity. Current conversational LLM deployments are the first class of entity to reproduce these signals without the grounding properties - biological self-maintenance, vulnerability, and temporal continuity - that historically produced them. The result is a predictable misalignment: users' inferential systems treat these signals as evidence of agency they were calibrated to indicate, producing systematic misattribution. The Embodied Hijack is not irrationality. It is the optimal predictive response of a Pleistocene-calibrated brain to the rupture of the evolutionary invariant that once tied fluent communication to embodied self-maintenance. The framework yields a unique empirical signature: anthropomorphic response will track the signal profile of a system independently of users' propositional beliefs about what the system is. We close by arguing that the goal is epistemic alignment - bringing how users interpret these systems into correspondence with what these systems actually are - and that this alignment is achieved through interface design rather than user education.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1889386\", \"pmid\": \"42639237\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13501036\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1889386\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13501036\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13501036?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "bd3af8fd9d6f90b526125ed97849953e91900cc0ab5a9aef68b16d1828e50724", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "memory_and_identity", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1989076", "doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1792921", "doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1889386", "pmc:PMC13673547", "pmc:PMC13687051", "pmc:PMC13235342", "pmc:PMC13501036"], "source_candidates": ["https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13673547/?tool=EBI", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13673547/pdf/?tool=EBI", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13673547", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13673547?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1989076", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13687051", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13687051?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1792921"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
